possum.origin: Possum fiber in textiles is the underfur of the common brushtail possum (Trichosurus vulpecula), an Australian marsupial introduced to New Zealand for a fur trade. It is not the American opossum (Didelphis), a different marsupial. In New Zealand the brushtail possum is officially a pest and, according to the Department of Conservation, the country's most damaging animal pest of native forest. Fiber enters the textile chain as a by-product of hunting and pest control, with fur recovered from the skins of killed animals. Because Predator Free 2050 aims to eradicate possums, a successful program would end this supply.
possum.structure: Brushtail possum fur is keratin with a scaled cuticle and cortex. Yarn makers describe the fibers as hollow and link this to low weight and warmth, but quantitative data on medulla or porosity are scarce in open literature, so those claims should be treated as producer statements. Measurements reported to the New Zealand Society of Animal Production (Reid et al., 2007) show strong variation by body region: belly fur averaged about 20 mm long and 16.2 microns in diameter, body fur about 27 mm and 17.7 microns, and tail fur about 38 mm and 22.9 microns, with belly fur also less curved. The short length explains why possum is blended.
possum.process: After harvest, fur is removed from the skins, graded by body region and color, and cleaned. It is then intimately blended, usually as a minority component, with merino wool and sometimes silk, cotton or cashmere, before carding and spinning. Yarn producers state that 100 percent possum yarn is not practical because the fibers are too short to hold together; the merino supplies length and cohesion while the possum adds loft and halo. Possum percentages vary by brand and must be read from the label. A New Zealand spinner describes developing specific carding and blending settings to keep the slippery fur from dropping out.
possum.performance: Possum-merino blends are marketed as lighter and warmer than wool alone; one producer claims a 55 percent warmth gain, a figure not traceable to a published standard test and best treated as marketing. Producers also claim strong pilling resistance attributed to the fiber surface; independent pilling data (for example Martindale or pilling-box tests) should be requested before relying on it. As keratin blends, these yarns absorb moisture vapor, char rather than melt, take acid dyes, and can felt or shrink in hot, agitated washing. Short possum fibers can shed from the yarn surface, especially early in wear.
possum.identify: Burn tests (indicative only; conduct with care) cannot separate possum from merino, since both are keratin. Microscopy can often distinguish marsupial underfur from sheep wool by scale pattern, diameter and medulla, but quantifying a minority possum share in a blend requires fiber counts under the microscope by a trained analyst, and DNA methods can confirm species. Buyers should not confuse New Zealand possum with opossum fur from the Americas or with rabbit hair, both of which also appear in soft, haloed blends.
possum.labeling: The FTC rule at 16 CFR 303.6 allows the name of a fur-bearing animal with the word fiber, hair or blend, for example possum fiber, when that fiber is 5 percent or more by weight, and otherwise the collective term fur fiber may be used when no claim about the animal is made. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 does not list possum among the named fine animal hairs, so it falls in the animal hair category, where the kind of animal may be indicated. Statements that possum products support conservation are environmental marketing claims that need evidence about the specific harvest.
possum.past: According to Te Ara, the Encyclopedia of New Zealand, the first releases of brushtail possums in 1837 failed, and a population was established in Southland in 1858. From 1858 to 1922 some 36 batches were imported, and by 1930 possums and their descendants had been released at about 450 locations. Hunting and selling skins were regulated until 1946, when all protection was removed after debate and the possum was treated as an environmental pest. Recovery of fur for blended knitwear grew later as a way to add value to control operations, and the government's Predator Free 2050 strategy now targets possums alongside rats and stoats.

rabbit.origin: Rabbit hair in textiles comes from the domestic rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus). The atlas separates it from angora: angora is the long wool of Angora breeds, harvested repeatedly from living animals and selected for fineness, whereas generic rabbit hair is typically the shorter fur of other breeds, often recovered from pelts and historically sold as fur for hat felt. Angora breeding research is active in China (for example the Wan and Zhexi strains) and has a history in France, while ordinary rabbit fur is a by-product of rabbit meat and pelt production.
rabbit.structure: Rabbit coats contain fine underfur and coarser awn and guard hairs. Rabbit hair is keratin, and under the microscope many fibers show a medulla made of rows of air-filled cells, often described as ladder-like, which makes the fibers light and insulating but lowers bending strength. Angora selection favors fine, weakly medullated fibers: an INRA study of French Angora rabbits measured the proportion of medullated fibers at only about 0.1 to 7.3 percent and a mean comfort factor (share of fibers at or below 30 microns) of about 97.5 percent. Ordinary rabbit fur is shorter and has more guard hair, which suits felting better than spinning.
rabbit.process: For hat felt, fur is separated from cleaned pelts, treated to improve its felting capacity, formed into a loose hood and consolidated by heat, moisture, acid and mechanical working before blocking and finishing. Historically, mercury compounds were used in this treatment, a step known as carroting, and exposed hatters to mercury. Where rabbit hair is spun rather than felted, it is usually blended as a minority share with wool or nylon because the smooth, short fibers shed and lack cohesion. Angora wool, by contrast, is harvested by shearing, combing or plucking and can be spun at high percentages.
rabbit.performance: Rabbit hair is very light and warm because of its air-filled medulla, and it felts readily, which is why it was prized for dense, smooth hat felts. In knitted yarns it produces a halo but tends to shed and to mat with abrasion and moisture. It absorbs water vapor like other keratin fibers, chars rather than melts, and dyes with acid dyes, though highly medullated fibers can dye paler. Low strength per fiber and short length mean that blends rely on the carrier fiber for durability. It is susceptible to moths and to felting shrinkage in hot, agitated washing.
rabbit.identify: Burn testing (indicative only; do it with care) shows typical hair behavior and cannot separate rabbit from other keratin fibers. Microscopy is more useful: the multi-row medulla and fine scale pattern are characteristic, and the near absence of medullation in fine angora helps separate it from rabbit fur rich in guard hair. Optical diameter analyzers such as OFDA measure diameter and comfort factor, but the INRA study found OFDA is not adapted to measuring medulla opacity or size in angora without special calibration.
rabbit.labeling: Under 16 CFR 303.6 the FTC permits the name of a fur-bearing animal with the word fiber, hair or blend when present at 5 percent or more, and the FTC's labeling guide gives Angora Rabbit Hair as an example of an acceptable disclosure; the term fur fiber may be used when no claim about the animal is made. In Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011, angora is reserved for hair of the angora rabbit, while other rabbit hair falls in the general animal hair category. Harvest method claims (shearing, combing or plucking) need documentation because the fiber does not reveal them.
rabbit.past: Rabbit fur was a major raw material of the felt hat trade. Its mercury hazard is well documented: Wedeen (1989) traces the first medical description of mercurialism in hatters to a report by J. A. Freeman in the Transactions of the Medical Society of New Jersey in 1860, and records that the tremor known as the hatters' shakes was rampant among immigrant workers. Medical findings did not end the practice; the occupational disease was curbed only in 1941, when mercury was required for detonators in World War II. Angora rabbit breeding for spinning wool developed separately and now includes genomic selection research.
